newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean police fire tear gas in first strike clash.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean police fire tear gas in first strike clash.

text.p: South Korean riot police fired volleys of tear gas at rock-throwing workers in Seoul on Saturday in the first violent clashes since strikes erupted across the nation two days ago.

Police unleashed barrages of tear gas canisters at about 5,000 workers to stop them marching down a busy thoroughfare to Myondong Cathedral in the city centre in protest at a new labour law, witnesses said.
Two police vehicles spraying tear gas from long nozzles saturated marchers, who responded by ripping up paving stones and hurling them at squads of officers.
Demonstrators set alight piles of banners and protest placards to keep police at bay and produce smoke to counter the effects of the stinging gas.
Bonfires flickered along a long stretch of road as protesters and police fought running battles.

Police waded into knots of chanting demonstrators and hauled away at least six people, witnesses said. They added that student radicals appeared to have infiltrated the protests and were responsible for some of the rock throwing.

Clashes broke out after the workers, many wearing red or blue protest headbands, broke away from a three-hour rally in a park where speakers denounced the government of President Kim Young-sam for passing the law in a clandestine session of parliament on Thursday.
"Overthrow the democracy-killing Kim Young-sam government," workers chanted.
The rally was organised by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
The government has condemned the stoppages as illegal and threatened unspecified "punishment" but has so far shown restraint in handling some of the worst industrial strife since the late 1980s.
"The new law will turn us into slaves, not workers. I am here to stop that from happening," said Kia Motors worker Chun Jong-il.
"The government is trampling on workers and the people. They aren't politicians -- they're thieves."

Snowballing industrial action that has devastated industry also threatens the financial sector. Banking unions announced a one day stoppage next Saturday and said a decision would be taken later on whether to extend the action.
But transport chaos was averted when non-union drivers kept trains running on the Seoul subway.
Nurses and orderlies at three more hospitals walked out, brining to 17 the number of medical centres forced to close all but emergency care.

The the government said stoppages that have almost completely idled car and ship production will cost the country more than $1 billion in lost production by the year's end. This was on top of $3.2 billion already lost through stoppages earlier in the year.
Unions claimed 375,000 workers at around 700 worksites had joined the walkout by Saturday. Two union umbrella bodies have called out their combined membership of 1.7 million.

Tellers and clerks at commercial banks and mutual savings firms feel vulnerable because financial market opening is expected to spark a wave of mergers in the heavily-protected industry, resulting in job cuts.
Next Saturday's strikes will also affect the central Bank of Korea.
Starting immediately, tellers and other unionised staff will refuse to wear uniforms.
Bank unions under the officially-recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions claim to represent 132,000 staff.
Underground trains in Seoul ran on time despite a strike by 9,000 drivers and ticketing staff.
The only inconvenience for an estimated four million passengers who use the system daily was closed ticket booths that forced them to use automated machines.
